#9960. Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways

Missing DMARC or wobbly SPF means your mail may be treated as suspicious

A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.

The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.

Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.

Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).

The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.

A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.

Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.

It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

#9959. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

After loading the model, you can do text-only inference with it as follows.

We would need torchvision to be able to use images and text.

Muse Glimmer accepts images as input, as demonstrated here:

To work with videos we recommend installing torchcodec into the environment.

Muse Glimmer can answer complex questions about videos without audio. You can do video inference as follows, here’s an example from VideoMME2, which is the most popular video question answering benchmark.

Muse Glimmer can do multimodal tool calling, here’s how you can do it. In the example below, we ask the model to call the weather tool based on the city in the image.

You can use Muse Glimmer to do open ended object detection in images as follows.

Here is an end to end script to perform object detection GitHub Gist

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:

Then you can start the server as follows.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:8080 to chat with the built-in WebUI.

You can also query the server as follows.

You can also use llama server with coding agents like Pi.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

Below you can see how speculative decoding can speed-up generation in realistic setups. The video shows llama.cpp webui with DFlash on the left and regular generation on the right.

You can load the drafter and model as follows, and infer like how you would with base model with an additional parameter (shown in the upcoming snippets).

You can start llama server using following command. --spec-draft-n-max argument controls how many future tokens DFlash proposes during each speculative-decoding step. Muse Glimmer’s DFlash model was trained with a block size of 16, one anchor token plus 15 proposed tokens, so any value above 15 will be clamped to 15.

You can also use llama cli with speculative decoding drafter as follows.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

The deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

As part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This shows how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

Set HF_TOKEN in the OpenClaw gateway environment, then add this to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Use the exact model ID returned by the endpoint’s /v1/models response if it differs.

If we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Muse Glimmer inspects the machine and Hub, selects or creates a Q4_K_M GGUF, launches llama-server, and validates model discovery and chat completion. The result is a smaller local build behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/Muse%20Glimmer%20Quantisation%20Demo%20-%20explained.mp4?download=true

By adding this to AGENTS.md openclaw or hermes will be able to solve the rest.

Muse Glimmer can also take care of the opposite. Let’s get Glimmer to deploy itself on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Which is useful if you want to speed up on some cutting edge hardware.

N.B. You can also just deploy Muse Glimmer to Inference Endpoints directly and connect your agent.

Muse Glimmer pins the model revision, deploys it to a protected Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, and verifies health, model discovery, and chat completion. It then connects the Claw agent with secrets and rollback preserved. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer will also need the Hugging Face MCP and/or the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

Muse Glimmer benchmarks its own single-H100 serving stack, testing one reversible change at a time while holding the workload fixed. It keeps only correctness-passing gains and finishes with the fastest reproducible configuration. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer need the Hugging Face MCP and the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/onyx-optimization-progress.gif?download=true

Try Muse Glimmer as a Hugging Face research agent. The Gradio Space sends each model request to a private Hugging Face Inference Endpoint through its OpenAI-compatible API. It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#9958. What is malloc doing, anyway?

malloc has a very nice and simple interface: you ask for a certain amount of memory, and you’re given a void pointer to your block of contiguous bytes that’s been magicked into existence. Once you’re done with it, you call free with the same pointer and the memory disappears into the ether.

But what’s actually happening here? Obviously, as we’re running as a userspace program, malloc must be asking the kernel for the memory through syscalls. However, we may be allocating many small blocks, and syscalls are expensive (575 ns for an empty one, as measured below), so some bookkeeping is done in the background. We’ll demonstrate this on GNU libc (glibc) with the program snippet below, which calls malloc(16) a thousand times.

Using strace, we can see that the whole loop makes only two brk syscalls: the first asks where the program break is (the address where the process’s heap ends), and the second grows the heap by 132 KiB. These are both done in the first malloc call — the other 999 just take from that already allocated memory.

You may see both brk and sbrk mentioned in discussions. brk is a syscall that sets the program break to the address it is provided, and sbrk is a libc convenience wrapper that takes a delta, increasing the program break by that amount.

A running process gets its own address space, split into a number of regions. These include text for executable code, data for initialised global variables, and bss for uninitialised global variables, among others. The following program prints one address from each region of the process.

The addresses rise from the binary’s code up to its stack.

Some of these regions can change as the program runs. For example, malloc(16) grows the heap and moves the break up. Note that in this run, the break and printf in libc are 23.4 TiB apart, about 1,530 times the machine’s 15.6 GiB of RAM. Nearly all of that range is unmapped, so it costs no physical memory.

Because we can move the program break directly, we can write a little allocator of our own. This is called a bump allocator, because each call simply bumps up the amount of memory that we are allowed to use.

This allocator is not very good! It moves the break on every single request, and each move is a syscall. We can time a syscall against malloc to see why malloc requests large blocks from the kernel and cuts them up itself. Each of the following three functions is timed over a million calls.

sbrk(16) costs only 35 ns more than the empty syscall, whereas malloc(16) runs 22.7 times faster than sbrk(16).

The bump allocator also has no way to reuse freed memory. Each request lands straight after the one before, so in the following example, d goes after c even though b has been freed.

The rest of the post improves the allocator one stage at a time.

malloc actually allocates more memory than you request. This is because each allocation, or chunk, has a size header just before the returned pointer; this is how free works without passing an explicit size. Chunk sizes are always multiples of 16, so the low bits of the size are always zero, and glibc keeps three flags in them.

Each chunk is the request plus 8 bytes for the header, rounded up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum of 32. The rounding keeps every pointer that malloc returns 16-byte aligned, which is the alignment x86-64 gives max_align_t, so the memory suits any C type. The 32-byte minimum leaves room for the list pointers that a chunk stores once it is freed.

When we free a chunk, it is put into what’s called a free list to allow reuse. When more data is requested, malloc looks through this free list and splits large chunks to fit small requests, and free merges free neighbours back together. Each chunk in the free list needs two pieces of information: its size (which we already have), and a pointer to the next chunk in the free list. glibc stores the pointer after the size, reusing the memory that the user stored their data in before it was freed!

The toy allocator stores the same two fields in each chunk.

We can improve our my_malloc by rounding the request plus its header up to a multiple of 16 bytes, and taking the first chunk in the free list that is big enough. To keep things simple, the toy’s header is the whole chunk_t, so a chunk keeps room for next even while it is in use. That makes the header 16 bytes where glibc’s is 8, and my_malloc(100) takes a 128-byte chunk where malloc(100) takes 112.

We define take to split that chunk, leaving whatever the request does not need in the free list.

When no free chunk fits, grow_heap moves the program break up in 64 KiB steps using sbrk and puts the new space on the free list as one chunk.

With headers, we can now actually implement a proper my_free function! It steps back from the pointer to the header and hands the chunk c to insert_free. That function walks the list to find the free chunks either side of c by address, prev and next, and links c in between them. Then, if c ends where next starts, or starts where prev ends, the two become one chunk.

A test program allocates a, b and c, frees a and b, allocates d, then frees the rest.

Each line shows the chunk that the call allocated, if any, and then the free list. Every chunk is an [offset, size] pair counted from the start of the heap, and the offset is where its header starts, 16 bytes before the pointer that my_malloc returns.

d gets the chunk at offset 0, split from the 352-byte chunk that a and b merged into. The bump allocator put its fourth request after everything else. Freeing c merges three chunks into one, and freeing d leaves the single 64 KiB chunk that grow_heap added.

my_free reuses memory, but it never returns any to the kernel. Whether a free chunk still costs RAM depends on when the kernel puts physical memory behind an address. Each process sees virtual memory, which the kernel maps onto physical RAM in 4 KiB pages. That separation allows the kernel to hand out address ranges with no physical RAM behind them — a virtual page only needs to be backed by physical memory on its first write.

The following program moves the break up by 1 GiB, then writes one byte to every page and prints a row after each 256 MiB.

Virtual size counts the addresses the process has mapped, and resident set size (RSS) counts the pages that are in RAM. Straight after sbrk, virtual size is already just over 1 GiB, while RSS is 1308 KiB. Each 256 MiB written then costs 65,536 page faults, one per 4 KiB page, increasing the RSS.

Once a chunk’s pages have been written, they stay resident after my_free, until the allocator gives them back to the kernel.

We give memory back to the kernel by lowering the break. We introduce a new function, trim, that lowers the break once the free chunk at the top of the heap reaches 128 KiB, keeping 64 KiB so that the next few requests don’t move the break straight back up.

A test program allocates 1 MiB and then a 16-byte chunk above it, then writes to every page of the 1 MiB block. (Anonymous RSS counts resident memory with no backing file, which keeps libc’s code out of the numbers.)

Freeing the 1 MiB block leaves the break at 1088 KiB and anonymous RSS at 1124 KiB, because the 16-byte chunk above it is still live. Once that chunk goes too, trim lowers the break to 64 KiB, dropping the anonymous RSS to 160 KiB.

Only the top of the heap can be given back. A live chunk holds the break above it, so every free chunk below it stays resident, as the 1 MiB block did here. Over a long run, many allocations and deallocations leave free gaps between live chunks that later requests rarely fill, which is called fragmentation. These gaps stay resident, so in a long-running program, fragmentation can grow RSS until a memory limit kills the process.

The mmap syscall usually maps a file into the address space. With the MAP_ANONYMOUS flag there is no backing file, and the kernel creates a zero-filled, page-aligned mapping anywhere in the address space. Like the heap, its resident pages count towards the anonymous RSS. The munmap syscall returns a block with its own mapping to the kernel as soon as it is freed, whatever lies next to it.

To integrate this into our own allocator, my_malloc chooses between sbrk and mmap by the size of the request. Any request of 128 KiB or more, header included, gets a mapping of its own from map_chunk, rounded up to whole pages; smaller requests take the existing sbrk free list path.

For mmapped chunks, we use one of the three flags in the size header (M) to record that this chunk has its own mapping. my_free checks this bit to know how to free it. It unmaps a mapped chunk with munmap, and puts any other chunk back on the free list, where trim can release it.

Running the previous demo again, we see that freeing the 1 MiB block drops the anonymous RSS while the 16-byte chunk is still live.

The following diagram shows how this might look in the address space.

Why not mmap everything? Some allocators do! Even glibc creates extra heaps, called arenas, with mmap, and spreads threads across them so that they don’t all contend for the lock on the main heap. However, separate mappings have separate regions with no guarantee of contiguity, and chunks can’t be coalesced across these gaps. On the other hand, allocating with sbrk just bumps up the one contiguous region that you already have. A freed chunk that stays on the heap keeps its pages resident, so reusing it causes no page faults. Each new mapping starts with no physical memory behind it, and faults on every page it writes.

We compare the performance of our allocators against glibc’s malloc with a workload that repeatedly allocates and deallocates blocks of varying sizes1. To measure the speed, we find the average time of a step: free a random live block, allocate a replacement of random size, and write to each of its pages. At the end of the run, the live blocks hold 10.3 MiB. The last two columns give the anonymous RSS at that point, and again after every block is freed, which is the memory the allocator keeps.

my-bump-1 never frees or reuses memory, so its RSS is the 1425 MiB that the run allocates in total. Its 1.72 µs per step comes from an sbrk call for every request and page faults on new pages. my-freelist-2 reuses memory, so its RSS of 17.8 MiB is much closer to the 10.3 MiB of live data. However, each step walks the list twice: my_malloc walks it to find a fit, and insert_free walks it to find the chunk’s neighbours. my-trim-3 adds a third walk, because trim looks for the last free chunk on every my_free. my-freelist-2 and my-trim-3 run 65 and 142 times slower than glibc respectively. In return, my-trim-3 keeps only 0.188 MiB once every block is freed. my-mmap-4 calls mmap for large requests, which raises its time per step to 11.8 µs but gives it the lowest RSS with blocks live, at 11.2 MiB.

Why is glibc so fast? The slowdowns in our allocators are due to having to walk a long free list of chunks multiple times. glibc instead keeps free chunks in bins, separate lists by size, so a request can walk a list of appropriately sized chunks directly. It also keeps up to seven freed chunks of each small size in a thread-local cache (tcache) and hands them straight back to the next request of that size.

The tcache also explains the last column, where glibc keeps 19.0 MiB after every block is freed. The heap counts a cached chunk as in use, so one near the top stops glibc from lowering the break. The GLIBC_TUNABLES environment variable can turn the tcache off with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0, or fix the mmap threshold at 128 KiB with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=131072.

With the tcache off, freeing everything leaves 0.250 MiB, and each step takes 1.5 times as long as before.

glibc makes 51 mmap calls in the whole run, against the 5040 that my-mmap-4 makes. Freeing a mapped chunk raises glibc’s threshold to that chunk’s size, so later large requests come from the heap. With the threshold fixed at 128 KiB, every large request pays for its syscalls and page faults again, and glibc runs 10.7 times slower.

malloc spends memory to stay away from the kernel, parcelling out large blocks in userspace so that most calls never make a syscall.

The benchmark keeps 4000 blocks live, and each step frees a random block and allocates a replacement of a random size. Of the requests, 90% are 16 to 512 bytes, 9% are up to 16 KiB, and 1% are 128 KiB to 256 KiB. Each new block gets one write per page. An allocator runs 500,000 steps in a fresh process, built at -O2. Run on an Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3. ↩︎

#9957. The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't

Infrastructure spending outruns measurable returns, with supplier finances key to judging when trouble arrives

The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices.

Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash.

"Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins.

"About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs."

Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare.

Its latest report, "An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register, have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use.

At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value.

A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity.

Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models.

If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist.

Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course.

Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says.

Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost.

But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains."

Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections.

Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.

Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL

Nov 07, 2026 3 min read

Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times.

According to the authors, pg_vectorsearch enables faster, more memory-efficient vector search directly in PostgreSQL, reducing the infrastructure required to handle large vector datasets. The extension supports existing pgvector columns, allowing applications to perform vector search without a separate database. To use the new capabilities, developers must install the extension and create a PRISM index on the vector column:

In Tiger Data’s own benchmarks using 100 million vectors, PRISM built an index in 1 hour and 40 minutes on a machine with 128 GB of memory, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) took 42 hours on a machine with 512 GB of memory. Formerly known as Timescale, Tiger Data is the company behind TimescaleDB, the open source PostgreSQL extension for time-series data and real-time analytics.

Erik Nordström, senior staff engineer at Tiger Data, Matvey Arye, principal engineer at Tiger Data, and Noah Hein, staff product marketing manager at Tiger Data, write:

PRISM brings a partition-based approach to PostgreSQL, similar to the approach used by newer dedicated vector search systems. Instead of connecting every vector to its neighbors in a graph, PRISM groups similar vectors into partitions and stores them as a list in a compressed format that is densely packed into database pages.

While HNSW is an approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm that quickly finds vectors similar to a query in large datasets, PRISM narrows searches to relevant partitions and scans compressed vectors sequentially. This reduces index size and avoids costly random memory or disk access, enabling faster vector search with less RAM directly in PostgreSQL.

Michael Freedman, cofounder and CTO of Tiger Data, published an article describing the architecture of the PRISM vector index. The index in pg_vectorsearch combines hierarchical clustering to narrow the search space, compressed vectors for efficient sequential scanning, and RaBitQ quantization to reduce expensive distance calculations. It duplicates vectors near partition boundaries to improve recall and relies on PostgreSQL’s native storage, logging, and concurrency mechanisms.

Incremental rebalancing is not yet fully implemented, so frequent data changes may require rebuilding the index to maintain search efficiency. Freedman explains:

The harder problem is maintaining the clustering as the dataset changes. Centroids don't automatically move when new vectors arrive, and posting lists gradually lose their original physical locality. We currently support limited on-demand splitting of oversized posting lists for flat indexes, but the more general rebalancing operations, including merging and reassignment, are not implemented yet.

In a popular Hacker News thread, the overall reaction is one of technical interest but caution. Practitioners see potential in faster vector search with lower memory requirements inside PostgreSQL, but raise questions about independent benchmark validation, whether pg_vectorsearch could replace pgvectorscale, and the lack of support for filtered searches. Hermon Hagos comments:

Vector search just got cheaper (...) For those of us building RAG apps on one database and a tight budget, that matters. Fast semantic search without spinning up a separate vector store or a bigger server is real money saved. It is still alpha, so do not ship it to clients yet, but this is one to watch closely.

Although not independently validated, Tiger Data’s benchmarks use an open source tool, measure recall@10 against exact search results, and compare both indexes under the same PostgreSQL configuration and instance types, using pgvector’s 16-bit halfvec for HNSW.

The new vector extension requires PostgreSQL 18 or later and currently supports vectors with up to 1968 dimensions. Filtered vector searches combining WHERE and ORDER BY are not supported until general availability. The project's code is available on GitHub. Tiger Data plans to move its existing pgvectorscale extension into maintenance mode.

#9955. Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

An unreleased version of the AI model has found and chained multiple vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux, Anthropic says.

An unreleased version of Claude identified critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used browsers and operating systems and chained them into working exploits requiring little or no human interaction, Anthropic said this week.

The exploits included one that enabled data theft from a locked Android smartphone, another zero-click exploit allowed remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on Linux servers, and a third that could have allowed attackers to remotely crash Windows systems. In total, Anthropic said, the model generated five working exploits targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. All affected vendors have addressed the vulnerabilities after Anthropic reported them.

The exploits are the latest evidence that frontier AI models are moving beyond simply identifying individual flaws to combining multiple into sophisticated working exploits. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said in a blog post this week.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Historically, creating such chained exploits would have required special teams with domain expertise, the researchers wrote. "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Anthropic's report described a one-click RCE exploit chain involving Chrome on macOS. The exploit combined four vulnerabilities in Chrome's JavaScript engine, memory protections, browser process isolation, and federated sign-in functionality.

Each of the vulnerabilities that Claude discovered helped overcome a different security control and allowed the chained exploit to escape the browser's sandbox. As a proof of concept, Anthropic's exploit launched macOS Calculator from Chrome when a user loaded a malicious webpage.

Anthropic said it reported 62 vulnerabilities to Google, all of which had been assigned CVE identifiers, rated high or critical, and patched by Chrome 156.

"For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers," Anthropic said. The exploit chain combined four weaknesses Claude identified in Safari — a use-after-free flaw in Safari's JavaScriptCore engine, a way to bypass WebKit's Gigacage memory protection, a vulnerability in the WebContent sandbox, and a JavaScriptCore flaw.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Apple has since fixed the issue, Anthropic said.

The Android exploit, meanwhile, targeted a locked Google Pixel 9. Claude chained three vulnerabilities in Android's device-transfer and USB-handling mechanisms, bypassing four layers of protection to extract photos and other personal information from the phone without unlocking it. Anthropic said Google has addressed the issue.

Claude's Windows exploit, which Microsoft has patched, involved a remotely exploitable denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. The flaw was an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's implementation of the transport protocol used by HTTP/3. An attacker could send a small number of specially crafted network packets to a vulnerable server to crash it and repeatedly trigger crashes, disrupting access for users, Anthropic said.

For Linux, Claude developed a zero-click exploit against the kernel's networking stack that would have let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute commands with root-level privileges on affected servers, without requiring any user interaction. "This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches," Anthropic said.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

With AI getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, defenders need powerful models for patching them before attackers can exploit the flaws, Anthropic said. "Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do," the company said.

To that end, the company is expanding access to its most capable AI models for vetted cybersecurity professionals through its Cyber Verification Program. The program now has three access tiers that give security teams a way to apply for the level of access appropriate for their work.

"It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward," Anthropic said. "Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever."

Andrew Bolster, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, says Anthropic's results are credible where they can be verified. The Chrome, WebKit, Windows, and Linux fixes are all public, he notes, but any claims that Claude discovered them autonomously are Anthropic's own. "The report gives no success rates, cost, or human-hours per chain, which is critical context for security leaders," he says.

Some of the conditions for the exploits to work were also noteworthy, he says. For instance, the Android chain involved a stolen phone and a USB cable, and the Linux exploit required an exposed MPTCP listener. "Exploit benchmarks show model success dropping sharply once ASLR, stack canaries, and sandboxing are enabled, and VulnCheck found only 1.3% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities confirmed exploited in the wild," Bolster says. "Delivery, reliability, and target preconditions remain the attacker’s problem for now, though I'd expect that gap to narrow."

Claude's chained exploits are another indication that AI has lowered the barrier to discovering vulnerabilities and building working attacks, says Jacob Krell, senior director, secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs. But there are still substantial barriers between a proof of concept and a reliable attack in the wild. "A shell on one honeypot tells you little about the next server's worker count, build, or kernel," Krell notes. "AI has made finding the bug cheap. Getting it to work on a server it has never seen is still the expensive part."

At the same time, the gap between a proof of concept and a reliable, broadly deployable attack is increasingly becoming about time and target-specific adaptation rather than specialized expertise, he cautions.

Defenders are making a mistake if they assume this kind of vulnerability discovery always requires the most powerful AI models, adds John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security. "Local systems, including a Mac Studio with 128GB of memory or a DGX Spark, can support AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research. The target, model, tools, and operator's skill matter."

It may take attackers longer, with less capable systems, and attacks may be more practical only against smaller, less-scrutinized code bases. But defenders need to account for that capability, Strand says. "If AI can find vulnerabilities in Windows, Android, Linux, and Chrome, what does that say about code that receives a fraction of that attention? Think about your IP cameras. Think about the firmware on the router running a remote office. All of that is in play."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. #9954. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#9953. Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

As artificial intelligence squeezes early-career learning opportunities, capture-the-flag contests could be one way to help pick up the slack.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed into their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, smart people have to backstop that work. And the only way these "humans-in-the-loop" can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem? With SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for security newbies to rack up real-world experience.

There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at software-as-a-service firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered up the spectacle and fun of an e-sports competition, but it may hold deeper clues as to how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile," he says. "If your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat. Doing CTF events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but they fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as Web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which started in 1996 and is still the event most associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries, competing for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes were dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept on reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests the money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, to build up expertise and exposure to its platform, and as a recruiting tool.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like amid a much broader spectrum of competitions available. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this past spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other more academic events, such as New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF, run versions aimed at students. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout corporate recruits.

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs evident in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI is going to do to the purpose and purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rule books and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, CSAW leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, requiring every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropped roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and the College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

SentinelOne's O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly 1,000 security leaders and found unclear career progression to be one of the top hiring challenges, cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only one-quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next, at 26%, with incident responders close behind, at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI's pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open source project Curl shut down their program after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month Google Bug Hunters also paused its open source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

An award-winning freelance reporter with nearly two decades of experience covering B2B cybersecurity, Ericka Chickowski has tackled every angle of security and risk for Dark Reading since 2009. Her coverage has spanned the full range of cyber topics important to every kind of cybersecurity stakeholder, including cybersecurity practitioners, CISOs, security-minded business managers, and security-aware board directors. She specializes in going deep on topics, breaking down how the technology trends affect real people, and how risk impacts the bottom line.

Some special areas of focus include: adversarial AI; AI risk and resilience; AI and agentic governance; application security (AppSec); governance, risk, and compliance (GRC); cloud security; network security; software supply chain risk; cyberinsurance; DevSecOps; enterprise risk management; and CISO career development.

#9952. Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed

UK shoppers caught up in third-party security mess, and nobody knows whether the data was flushed away

Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia.

In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register, the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider.

The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on.

The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper.

Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question.

"We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse.

In a separate public statement, Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed.

Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications.

"The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email.

While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions.

Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided."

Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

#9951. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#9950. Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series discusses some of the trends and topics from Cybersecurity Awareness Month, from using AI for better training to educating next-generation workforces on modern risks and emerging threats.

AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system.
