#9895. unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world

Co-founder of Assetnote, security researcher.

I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before (previous works), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au:

Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au. What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that:

Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle.

Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate.

When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au, and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc).

So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for.

The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au, we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au. This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform.

This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱:

Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too.

Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/*.

Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible).

Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway.

I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be?

Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/, and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work:

But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/, thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so:

In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT.

We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully.

All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following:

These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way?

What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail, guid, and phone. Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do?

The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded.

Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre.

Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it.

It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination.

When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/, we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue.

With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile:

OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication?

Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app:

We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session:

Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token:

It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app.

At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone.

We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with.

But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this:

At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these.

You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives?

There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here. It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments.

At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

#9894. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

InfoQ Homepage Articles Agentic AI Architecture: Current Challenges and Future Opportunities

Nov 09, 2026 11 min read

Most software engineers and architects are innately familiar with microservices and cloud-native architectures and have been involved in building systems based on these architectures for many years. Microservice-based systems tend to consist of tens or hundreds, and sometimes even thousands of services, responsible for different types of data processing, be it API endpoints, data pipelines, back-office workflows, and anything in between, but they do have one thing in common - they merely process data using a logic determined either by code or based on data retrieved from data stores. This doesn’t mean that such systems are simplistic - far from it. Still, despite their complexity, they can be reasoned about deterministically, which helps define and scope functionality, implement and test changes, and operate such systems, even in the face of infrastructure- or application-level failures.

All of this is about to change. Indeed, a good share of future software systems will still be deterministic and resemble what we are used to today. Still, quite soon, swathes of IT systems being designed and delivered will be leveraging AI-based solutions to power user-facing functionality. For most, if not all, architects and engineers, this will require significant adaptation to the new reality of the IT industry.

Automated code transformation at scale. Fix vulnerabilities, migrate frameworks, and modernize legacy code across every repo. Try Moderne Free.

The adoption of AI in software architectures is driven primarily by the new capabilities that it offers, which are particularly useful for products used by knowledge workers. Historically, IT systems focused on storing, processing, and making data available via APIs and user interfaces. At the same time, humans were responsible for a good portion of data administration, utilizing business rules, procedures, office "tribal" knowledge, and their own judgment. It’s fair to point out that some, or even much, of this intelligence was built directly into IT systems to improve productivity, particularly when scaling business operations was critical. With AI-enabled capabilities, software systems can shift from operating on raw data to knowledge, thereby elevating IT's role from merely a data management and processing function to knowledge-level support for business operations and end-user functionality.

It’s difficult to gauge to what extent AI-based solutions will dominate next-generation software systems. Still, by all signs, the impact will be so substantial that we can speak about a new type of software architecture, one where AI powers large areas of functionality, making humans using products built on top of next-generation systems much more productive. Agentic AI Architecture is a software architecture in which agentic AI systems are leveraged on a substantial scale, geared towards making optimal use of generative AI (and other) models. This type of architecture builds on microservices and cloud-native architecture and adds agentic AI capabilities.

Agentic AI isn’t exactly new, but equally, it’s not yet well established either. Over the last couple of years, agentic AI systems have evolved from simple, single-agent solutions to chains, to graphs and multi-agent systems (MAS), where multiple agents collaborate, organized in various topologies. This area is still undergoing active development, and more elaborate use cases will inevitably emerge. It’s fair to say, though, that different collaboration strategies or topologies work best for specific use cases, so choosing a simpler solution can be advantageous in many cases.

Agents make the most of the large language models (LLMs) they interact with by providing the right context. Here again, after starting with predefined prompts, the solutions gradually shifted to a dynamic context based on output from other agents, context propagation, or data fetched from external sources via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

As the amount of context accumulated from different sources began to cause problems with diminished reasoning, engineers developed new ways of managing context, and context engineering emerged as a separate practice. The progressive context disclosure technique can further enhance the context preparation step by allowing the agent to selectively load detailed information into the context window based on the user’s prompt.

Since LLMs have effective limits on context size, the role of context engineering is to ensure that the context used maximizes the model's likelihood of producing the desired outcome, or at least minimizes the chance of hallucinations due to vague or inadequate context. Effective context engineering requires context management to store, optimize, and reuse context elements for subsequent agent invocations.

Lately, memory systems for AI agents have also emerged, enabling further enhancements to context editing. These systems organize different types of long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) for storage and querying, thus allowing agents to supplement the context with past experiences/decisions, relevant facts/definitions, rules, or learned behaviors.

Context engineering has become a foundational architectural concern for agentic AI systems. It will undoubtedly continue to evolve as the needs and expectations for building and operating AI-based products grow.

Agentic AI has developed its own specialized set of communications protocols. This process was largely driven by challenges related to the complexity of agent development, the need for standardization, and the need for improved interoperability:

For agentic AI systems to be valuable, they need to be integrated into a bigger enterprise architectures. In the enterprise setting, incorporating an agentic AI system can be done by:

A large-scale enterprise-level architecture may comprise many specialized agentic AI systems. Since AI agents can use MCP to use database, services/APIs or any arbitrary data sources directly, it’s important to ensure that their interactions are constrainted within a bounded context, as defined by the domain-driven design (DDD). Limiting the reach of agentic AI systems within larger architectures reduces coupling between distant or unrelated components and data sources, allowing more cohesive areas to be maintained by engineering teams without excessive dependencies or large blast radius if changes are introduced.

Figure 1: Multiple Agentic AI Systems in Separate Bounded Contexts (Source: created by the author)

Figure 1 (above) depicts somewhat simplified architecture with two bounded context, each one embedding an agentic AI system with multiple agents (A), as well as other microservices (S). Agents only use local data sources and services for context expansion or as tools, hence limiting the coupling with other parts of the boarder software system.

The scalability of cloud-based software architectures is well understood, as architects and engineers have been building and operating them for some time. The same can’t be said for agentic AI systems, where LLM call latencies are higher, and more complex multi-agent systems can further increase processing times. The performance of agentic AI systems can’t be measured solely by standard metrics such as throughput, latency, or error rates.

Researchers at Google and MIT published a paper introducing a framework for scaling multi-agent systems. The team behind the framework tested various multi-agent coordination strategies, each with several configuration parameters, including the number of LLM calls, agents, and interactions per agent. Scientists concluded that the best coordination strategy is task-dependent: financial reasoning does better with centralized orchestration, while web navigation benefits from a decentralized strategy.

The results shared by Google and MIT demonstrate that there is no one-size-fits-all approach when it comes to agentic AI, and teams building complex solutions have to experiment and empirically establish the agent coordination strategy that is best suited to the task.

Incorporating agentic AI into the distributed system architecture significantly alters the security model. Agentic AI contributes additional security threats, particularly around the agent runtime, tool servers (MCP or others), and the model provider. AI agents, for instance, can be susceptible to prompt injection, instruction confusion, or tool output poisoning, leading to unintended actions or leaking data they have access to. Additionally, using external LLM models introduces risks around data residency, retention, or usage.

Furthermore, present access-control models, honed over many decades, are ill-suited to cater to agents, which can’t really be treated as human users or backend services. Cameron Pavey, senior developer at Auth0, recently proposed a new permission model specifically targeting AI agents. He argues that regular (non-AI) backend services are generally more trusted because they are deterministic and auditable, while authentication sessions and user interfaces restrict users. Agents, on the other hand, can arbitrarily trigger multi-step workflows that involve other agents and tool calls without the user’s explicit knowledge or permission.

Pavey proposes using capability-scoped permissions and task-scoped credentials as key steps toward solving the problem of agent permissions and adopting fine-grained authorization systems for layered enforcement.

It’s worth pointing out that this is not the first time that the security landscape has experienced a marked expansion. When microservices and cloud-native architectures entered the scene, we observed a shift in this area as well, leading to a revision of the access control mechanism and protocol and the emergence of now-common technologies such as JWT and OAuth.

Considering the non-deterministic nature of agentic AI systems, observability is key to being able to effectively build, enhance, troubleshoot and operarate them.

Teams should aim at complete coverage across all pillars of modern observability platforms:

Despite the expected rise of agentic AI as the driving force behind future IT products and services, we cannot expect an instant switch. For many years, the distributed systems architectures we know today will coexist with the next-generation ones (which build on top of them), similar to how service-oriented architecture (SOA) was phased out in favor of microservices over a few years.

Additionally, given the relative infancy of agentic AI, this space will take time to mature and gain widespread adoption, allowing for a gradual transition and the emergence of new patterns, best practices, and technologies that will further drive adoption.

Finally, not all products or business processes need to leverage agentic AI, or the use of AI may not be immediately financially viable. It may be that certain industries or classes of products or systems will not benefit from AI at the same pace as others. In that sense, microservices and cloud-native architectures are here to stay in one way or another.

With Agentic AI taking center stage and maturity and adoption within the industry growing, I expect many components and solutions, currently often custom-built, to be offered as features of more generic platforms that will support multi-agent system delivery and operations, as well as the integration of those into broader enterprise-level architectures.

In particular, foundational agentic AI building blocks, such as agent memory, asset registry, guardrails, and orchestration, as well as support for observability and operations, should all become built-in capabilities of agentic AI platforms, whether homegrown or offered by vendors or cloud providers.

There are several agentic AI platforms/frameworks that developers can use today, including LangChain (with LangGraph), CrewAI, Azure AI Foundry, Google Agent SDK (ADK), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

This process will follow the same path as it did for microservice architectures, where growing needs from organizations adopting these new architectures have necessitated the creation of internal, self-operated solutions that externally hosted and managed products will gradually replace.

The industry is on the verge of a major shift, and Agentic AI Architecture has a strong chance of becoming a dominant architecture for distributed systems over the coming years and decades. This doesn’t mean that microservices and cloud-native architectures will become obsolete; rather, they will form the basis of the next generation of systems, in which AI powers much of the user experience. What architects and engineers are familiar with today will form a foundation for delivering robust AI-powered products and services that combine data, knowledge, and compute-based reasoning.

The shift described here will increase productivity and improve ease of use for many knowledge workers across many sectors. It will greatly reshape not only the IT industry but our entire modern society.

While we are still in the early days, with a lot of innovation, moving goalposts, experimentation, and learning, we can certainly expect an exciting road ahead.

#9892. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

#9890. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

The image-based OS approach enables us to enforce some very strict but powerful security properties, which elevate the security posture of the system substantially above traditional Linux systems. Specifically, let's highlight seven major essential security properties of AOS here: No Shell + No SSH + No Language Interpreters. By default AOS does not install a UNIX shell, nor makes remote access via SSH available on the nodes. Moreover, we do not install any of the usual language interpreters (Python, Perl, …) by default. For most nodes a shell or interpreted language support is not required and it removes a whole class of attacks. Signed Images Only. #9888. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

#9887. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

#9886. Asahi Linux 7.3 progress report

Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. #9885. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks, but it doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

And the CPU is parallel, but not as parallel as a GPU. So, long story short, smaller models, which basically make sense to run in a browser, for instance, do make sense to run in WebAssembly, much bigger workloads... Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. So, TornadoVM is, we could say a flavor of the JVM or an add-on, a plug into the JVM, depends on how you see it. TornadoVM allows you to run Java code essentially on the GPU. It's called the VM because it allows you to translate on the fly your Java code, and compile it on the fly into GPU-specific kernels. So, PTX for NVIDIA, SPEAR-V, whatever. Olimpiu Pop: That sounds quite interesting, and it definitely makes sense these days. Today, you are part of the team at Red Hat, back again at Red Hat, that is working on llm-d. And in my understanding, what llm-d is, taking a step back, if VLLM is making sure that everything runs perfectly on one box, llm-d is trying to make sure that everything is efficient if you have a Kubernetes cluster. Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.

So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.

Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.

If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.

But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.

But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.

We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. So you can schedule request to do batch processing in the background when your cluster is underused because basically this hardware is so expensive that you want to keep it at 100% all the time. So even when there is no live inference going on, you can schedule batch processing to run when you're sleeping when there's less work to be done live. So that's what llm-d does. It uses your hardware as much as possible so that the money you spend gets you the best value and you do it on your own hardware so you can do inference without leaking data to a third party, which is important these days.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. It allows you to make cloud native inference and evolve your infrastructure in such a way that you can do AI on-premises, in a similar way as you did cloud native development before AI.

Olimpiu Pop: Well, that was always an issue, but now it feels that we are discussing in the cloud-native; most of the times we spoke about stateless. Whenever you call something, you didn't always ring on the same doorbell because that was one issue. Another issue was in the Kubernetes space, it was the part with I/O, well, most particularly persistent data, like database and stuff like that. Whenever you spoke to infrastructure guys, they told you, "Well, we can have everything in Kubernetes except for databases because then those things become more complex." But let's take them one by one. How do you bring in a stateless ecosystem like Kubernetes, worked a lot in Bing, something that theoretically should be stateful?

Because if I have a conversation, I would like to continue my conversation about, I don't know, whatever stupid thing I speak to Gemini or Cloud or OpenGPT or whatever stuff, I don't want to have my responses coming for what Eduardo was speaking to his LLM.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, it's a complex problem for sure. As I said, one part of the story is that... Well, I mean, if people that are hearing that the audience know how LLM generally work, essentially the stateful nature of the LLM in a way is fake, in that they are really stateless. The way they do inference is that we send them the entire history of a conversation every single time. So, maybe I jumped at-

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, to the conclusion earlier. And I said a lot about prefix caches and KV caches, but yes. So, essentially the way an LLM works is that essentially you always send the entirety of the conversation to the LLM. And what really happens is the LLM completes the conversation. I don't know if people recall how OpenAI and the GPT Lab playground worked a few years ago. Basically, it was the completion API. You wrote a sentence and then the LLM wrote the continuation of that. And the cool thing was that someone discovered if you wrote that prompt as a conversation, as a dialogue with quotes, user says da, da, da, computer says... The LLM will continue the conversation. And that's how ChatGPT basically was born. People notice this, and notice this pattern.

Now, LLMs are being trained with this pattern, but that's how basically originally it work. So, if you think of it this way, every conversation really is a very long prompt to the continuation of that conversation. The way LLM works, you send the history of the conversation and then they continue with the next answer, and then you get back the answer, and then you continue with your answer, and so on, so forth, so on and so forth. If you are using LLMs, you will know that pricing for these things, depending if you're using token-based spend or a subscription... Well, if you're using a subscription, that doesn't really matter. But if you're using token-based pricing, you will know that there's a difference between cached responses and responses.

The reason is, if you don't do a cached response, then you are sending the entire history of your conversation to the LLM. The LLM does not have that conversation in cache, so it will have to do inference on the entire prompt, and that's why that will be particularly expensive. But if you've been going back and forth for a while without long pauses and the cache on the server has not been evicted, then you've been reusing stored cache estate to continue the conversation. That does not mean necessarily that you haven't sent the entire history to the LLM, it just means that even though you are sending the entire history, the history is recognized as part of a prefix of a cache, and so the LLM can compute only the continuation instead of the entire prompt.

So, we have these mechanism for caching in place so that basically LLMs, if the cache exists, can only infer the last few tokens that continue the conversation instead of have to re-compute the entire state from the prompt. llm-d does that for you. So, it maintains this cache both in the form of a KV cache, with one going to the deals how that works, and a prefix cache. And both these caching mechanism allow you to persist the state across the exchanges in your conversation, persist as in volatile memory because these are caches... Usually they're not persistent for a long time. And that's the reason also why you want to stick usually to the same VLLM instance, even though llm-d also gives you ways to move around across instances. It's a lot, we cannot explain how all that works. But in general, llm-d allows you to do this, allows you to have an efficient use and even for stateful conversation of your hardware.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay. So, llm-d, it's also donated, if I remember correctly, to the CNCF Foundation, right?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. It recently reached 1.0 a few days ago. Yes.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay, congratulations. So, we are right in time. In what state is it? Is it production ready? Should we wait for it?

Edoardo Vacchi: Oh no, it's definitely production-ready, there's a number of companies that are already using it. At Red Hat, we're actually partners with NVIDIA for a bunch of things. We have a lot of success stories already, people using it in production. And yes, you should definitely take a look at it. In fact, sometimes I go to conferences and I realize people are already using it, or maybe they're using VLLM on their infrastructure and they're not aware of llm-d. So, VLLM allows you to do inference up to a degree in a very high performance, high quality way, and the llm-d and VLLM projects are sister projects in a way. I mean, there's a lot of exchanges across the stack, so we are part of the same team in a way. But yes, llm-d gives you that edge. For instance, VLLM does not do automatic flow control, even if you are only running a one VLLM instance, llm-d gives you control over quality of service and prioritization of HTTP requests.

So, that is something that VLLM, at least until a few days ago, I don't know if things have changed recently, could not do. So, you can get benefit from llm-d even if you're not necessarily running in a very highly distributed situation.

Olimpiu Pop: So, what does that mean? Even if you don't have a cluster, use llm-d?

Edoardo Vacchi: Even if you don't have a lot of GPUs, even if you don't have to distribute the load across different GPUs, llm-d might still be useful. And yes, you can also run it bare metal. So, you might want to evaluate llm-d even if you're not using Kubernetes. I mean, Kubernetes is the first target, but it is supported also on bare metal.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay. So, it's focusing on inference, even if you don't have already existing infrastructure. It seems that at the point when we are recording this, it's end of October, and it seems that llm-d started at the end of October in 2024.

Olimpiu Pop: So, it's a good moment to have the first major version out in this period. So, congratulations.

Olimpiu Pop: But staying in the Kubernetes space, one of the reasons why people prefer to use things that they are already familiar, Kubernetes is not that old of a solution comparing to other types of solution that were out there, but it's still one of the most mature in the cloud native space.
