#9838. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

#9837. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:Video Call Exploit Chains Two Flaws in Unisoc Modems

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9835. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9833. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and, sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: So this one was pretty interesting, and in the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, I think it's extremely relevant. The story came out from The Athletic about a week and a half ago, two weeks now almost, that the NBA champion New York Knicks — credit to them, I'm a Celtics fan, I hate the Knicks but, you know, good for them, they won the championship last year — that employees from the team apparently got a phishing test email saying your employee championship ring is here and that they could choose, you know, from different types of championship rings no cost to the employees, and when the employees clicked on the link they were informed that they had failed a phishing test and that they would have to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: TornadoVM, A2A Java, Open Liberty, Open J Proxy, Gradle, EclipseStore

Nov 09, 2026 4 min read

This week's Java roundup for November 2nd, 2026, features news highlighting: point releases of TornadoVM, TornadoInsight, A2A for Java, Gradle and EclipseStore; the November 2026 edition of Open Liberty; the third release candidate of Open J Proxy; the second release candidates of Micrometer Metrics and Micrometer Tracing; and the third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.

Build 23 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 22 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The release of TornadoVM 8.1.0 delivers bug fixes and notable changes such as: the ability for a TornadoVM kernel read and write a device allocation owned by another library owns, in place, without copying it and without writing a TornadoVM array header into it; and a change in the overloaded initializeDeviceAsync() method, defined in the TornadoExecutionPlan class, to initialise a device during application sets up. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Beehive Lab has also released version 2.1.0 of TornadoInsight, their IntelliJ IDEA plugin for TornadoVM. This release includes bug fixes, documentation improvements and new features such as: a new experimental AI-assisted transformation of a Java method into a TornadoVM kernel; and a new TornadoToolchain record that checks the TornadoVM SDK with the project JDK, builds the classpath, compiles with the project JDK, and creates a launcher. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of A2A Java SDK 1.5.0, a Java library that implements the Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) for running agentic applications as A2AServers, ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new OpenTelemetryPushNotificationSenderDecorator class to create a CLIENT enumeration, defined in the OpenTelemetry SpanKind enum class, to reflect the actual delivery outcome of success or failure; and the ability for authorized JPA task listings to offer optional provider capabilities so that supported policies can directly filter both the database count and page queries that for reduced scan and deserialization costs. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for Valkey in the Quarkus Redis Client extension; and a new @CheckedTemplateParam annotation to support explicit naming of parameters in methods annotated with @CheckTemplate without the required -parameters compile flag. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The GA release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.11 delivers bug fixes, resolutions to numerous CVEs and new features such as: the ability to configure the timeout of the server quiesce stage, via the quiesceTimeout element, that was once fixed at 30 seconds; and improved validation that blocks form login error page redirects to external hosts unless the target host is listed in the wasReqURLRedirectDomainNames attribute of the element.

The third release candidate of Open J Proxy 1.1.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for PostgreSQL and MariaDB coverage in the C++ ODBC client; and a simplification of building and using the C++ ODBC drivers across all major OS platforms. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of Gradle 9.9.0 provides notable changes such as: the ability for Kotlin DSL scripts to be incrementally compiled using the Kotlin Build Tools API for improved build performance; new test filters that may be applied to JUnit Platform tests that are not declared as methods; and improvements to the Problems API that provides a predefined hierarchy of problem groups from the Problems interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of EclipseStore 4.3.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: A refactor of the VectorIndex interface, part of the JVector Index, to handle large indices and concurrent load and crash safety; and a new, lightweight VanillaJS storage viewer for the storage REST Interface that now deprecates the existing standalone Vaadin/Spring-based client GUI. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The second release candidate of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 ships with dependency upgrades and one new feature that adds support for fractional updates in Micrometer Atlas counters that had previously truncated them to a type long. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the second release candidate of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: more efficient allocation of OpenTelemetry baggage reads by directly searching retained/current baggage and building the bulk results in one map; and an elimination of allocating wrappers while clearing an already empty context by reusing the NOOP function, defined in the CurrentTraceContext.Scope interface in conjunction with an instance of the Tracer.SpanInScope interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Andres Almiray, Java Champion and creator of JReleaser, has introduced his roadmap for JReleaser 2.0. Over the next several weeks, developers can expect changes that include:

A 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT release has been created and there will be numerous breaking changes.

#9830. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9828. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9827. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9825. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9823. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎
