#9773. How to Trace AI Agent Decisions Across Blockchain Transactions

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

A blockchain transaction can tell us what happened. It cannot, by itself, explain why an AI agent decided to initiate it. Imagine an AI agent monitoring a decentralised finance application. It reads wallet balances, retrieves liquidity data, evaluates a possible transaction, calls a smart contract, and waits for confirmation. Eventually, the transaction appears on-chain. A monitoring dashboard shows its hash, gas consumption, status, and block number. Everything looks normal.

Then someone notices that the transaction moved assets into a position the user never intended to create. Where did things go wrong? Perhaps the agent interpreted an instruction incorrectly. Perhaps an RPC provider returned stale information. Perhaps the market changed after the agent calculated the expected outcome. Perhaps a policy check passed against an outdated configuration. Or perhaps the transaction executed exactly as designed, but the design itself failed to account for an important condition.

The transaction hash does not answer these questions. Neither does a conventional application log that says a tool call succeeded. To investigate the incident, engineers need to reconstruct the complete path from the original instruction to the final on-chain state. They need to understand which information the agent observed, how it interpreted that information, what action it proposed, which controls approved the action, and what happened during execution. This is where I believe observability needs to evolve.

My work and writing around production AI have repeatedly brought me back to a distinction that is easy to overlook: making a system capable of performing a task is not the same as making its behaviour understandable when something goes wrong. AI agents introduce additional uncertainty because they can select tools, generate plans, and change their approach based on intermediate results. Blockchain introduces another layer of complexity through asynchronous transactions, external data dependencies, network conditions, and state changes that may be difficult or impossible to reverse. Combining the two creates a system that needs visibility into both reasoning-related decisions and deterministic execution.

Blockchain applications need an observability layer that connects what an AI agent intended to do with what the infrastructure actually executed. That layer should not attempt to expose every internal model computation or turn private reasoning into an audit log. It should capture the operational evidence needed to explain decisions, enforce policies, investigate failures, and verify outcomes.

Traditional blockchain monitoring has a well-understood job. It tracks transactions, blocks, contract events, network health, gas usage, and other indicators of execution. These measurements remain essential. They tell us whether transactions were submitted, whether they were included in a block, whether execution succeeded, and how the network behaved. But consider what happens before an AI-generated transaction reaches the blockchain.

An agent receives a request, retrieves context, calls one or more tools, interprets their responses, evaluates possible actions, and produces a transaction proposal. That proposal passes through authorisation, signing, and submission before the blockchain processes it. Every stage can introduce a different failure. The agent may select the wrong contract. A retrieval service may provide outdated protocol information. An RPC provider may become unavailable. A policy engine may reject a valid transaction because it received malformed input. A signer may refuse an operation that exceeded their authorisation. The transaction may be accepted by an RPC endpoint but remain pending, or it may be included in a block and revert during execution.

A dashboard focused exclusively on the blockchain sees only part of this journey. Likewise, an AI application log may record that the model proposed a swap without establishing whether the proposal was authorised, signed, submitted, or confirmed. The problem is not that either monitoring system is inadequate within its own domain. The problem is that the two systems often describe different parts of the same operation without a shared way to connect them. An AI-native observability layer bridges that gap. It connects the original request, the agent's operational decisions, the data used to support those decisions, the policy checks, the transaction lifecycle, and the resulting on-chain state. The goal is not to replace blockchain explorers, node metrics, or application monitoring. It is to connect their evidence into a single operational picture.

Logs are useful for recording individual events. A service might log that it retrieved a balance, generated a transaction proposal, or received a transaction receipt. The difficulty begins when an operation crosses several services.

Suppose an agent retrieves data through an RPC gateway, obtains additional information from an indexer, sends a proposal to a policy service, and submits an approved transaction through a signing service. Each component produces its own logs, often with its own request identifiers and timestamps.

During an incident, engineers may have to search several systems and manually reconstruct the order of events. If an intermediate request was retried, if a response arrived late, or if the agent resumed a workflow after a timeout, that reconstruction becomes even harder. A timestamp alone is not enough to establish causality. Two events can occur close together without belonging to the same workflow, while events from one workflow may appear out of order because different services process them asynchronously.

This is why distributed tracing is a useful foundation. OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral model for collecting traces, metrics, and logs across instrumented services. A trace can represent a larger operation, while individual spans describe the work performed by its components. For a blockchain-connected agent, one trace might represent the attempt to execute a particular user request. Its spans could include context retrieval, transaction planning, policy evaluation, simulation, signing authorisation, RPC submission, and receipt verification. The resulting trace gives engineers a structured way to understand how the operation progressed. However, a trace alone does not establish that the operation was correct. It establishes the relationships between recorded operations and helps reveal where failures or delays occurred.

The observability layer must therefore combine tracing with domain-specific information: transaction identifiers, chain and block references, policy versions, execution status, and the outcome that the user originally requested.

I would design the architecture around six connected layers.

The diagram represents a logical architecture rather than a requirement to deploy every component as a separate service. A small application might implement several layers within one process. A larger platform may distribute them across multiple services. What matters is that each stage has a defined responsibility and emits enough structured evidence for the next stage to be observed.

The runtime records when an agent begins a task, which tools it invokes, how long each operation takes, and whether the agent produces a proposal or requests additional information. For example, the runtime might record that an agent evaluated three transaction routes, rejected two under its configured constraints, and selected the third for further validation.

It does not need to capture the private chain of thought or every intermediate token. It needs a concise operational record of the decisions and outputs that matter to the workflow.

The context layer records where decision-relevant information came from. For blockchain data, useful attributes may include the chain ID, block number, block hash, source provider, observation timestamp, and indexing checkpoint, where applicable.

These attributes help engineers determine whether an agent acted on current and consistent information. A block number should not be treated as a universal freshness guarantee. The system must also consider the network's finality characteristics, the source's progress, and the requirements of the specific operation.

The policy layer records which rules were evaluated and whether the proposal passed. Useful fields include a policy version, the result of each relevant check, a machine-readable rejection reason, and whether additional authorisation was required. This allows an investigator to distinguish between an agent that proposed an invalid action and a policy engine that incorrectly authorised it.

Sensitive policy details should be access-controlled. The observability system should not become a convenient source of information for someone attempting to bypass security controls.

The execution layer records the transition from proposed transaction to authorisation, submission, inclusion, and verification. The distinction between these states matters. A successful RPC response does not necessarily mean that a transaction was confirmed. A receipt with a successful execution status is stronger evidence of execution, but the application may still need to verify that the resulting state satisfies the original goal.

The final layer compares the intended outcome with the observed result. If the agent intended to transfer a specified amount to an approved destination, the system should verify the relevant transaction and state changes rather than relying solely on a success message returned by the execution service. For more complex operations, such as adjusting a DeFi position, the expected outcome may involve several balances, contract events, and protocol-specific state variables.

The verification rules should be defined for the application rather than inferred solely from the model's natural-language summary.

Traces, metrics, and structured audit records feed dashboards, alerts, incident investigations, and recovery workflows. An alert might identify repeated RPC failures, a growing number of transactions stuck in a pending state, an increase in policy rejections, or a mismatch between confirmed transactions and expected business outcomes.

The objective is to move beyond reporting that something failed and toward identifying which boundary failed, what evidence supports that conclusion, and what safe action should happen next.

Consider a hypothetical agent that is asked to exchange a limited amount of a stablecoin for another asset. The agent retrieves the wallet balance, queries a liquidity pool, calculates an expected output, and proposes a swap. The policy engine checks the spending limit and slippage tolerance. A secure signer authorises the validated transaction, and an RPC endpoint submits it. A useful trace should preserve the relationships between these operations.

This trace is illustrative. In a real implementation, some stages may run concurrently, be retried, or occur in separate traces linked through workflow identifiers. The important feature is the relationship between them. An investigator should be able to start with a failed transaction and work backwards to the exact proposal, policy decision, and observations that supported it. Equally, the investigator should be able to start with an agent decision and follow it forward to the transaction's outcome.

A trace should also distinguish between attempts and logical operations. If an RPC request is retried three times, those attempts should remain visible without making them look like three separate user requests. This distinction becomes particularly valuable when agents resume long-running workflows. A workflow may survive a process restart, wait for a transaction to be included in a block, and continue later. Its operational history should remain connected even if its execution crosses several processes or sessions.

For a production system, I would use a durable workflow or operation identifier to connect the lifecycle, while creating spans for individual execution attempts. Where operations cross tracing boundaries, trace context can be propagated through service calls or linked explicitly. There is one important limitation: traces can be sampled, dropped, or retained for shorter periods than audit records. A security-sensitive application should not rely on sampled traces as its sole record of financial authorisation or execution.

Observability and auditability overlap, but they serve different purposes. Traces help engineers investigate behaviour. A durable audit record preserves the evidence required to establish what the system authorised and executed.

An observability design becomes more useful when it can be implemented with ordinary engineering tools. The following Python example uses OpenTelemetry-style instrumentation to create a trace for an agent's blockchain read. It illustrates how an application can associate a chain identifier and block reference with a request. The RPC response parsing and provider implementation are intentionally left outside the example because those depend on the application's client library.

This is a simplified instrumentation example, not a complete production RPC client. The actual method signature, block-reference format, and error handling must match the provider library being used.

It also deliberately avoids recording the wallet address or balance as unrestricted span attributes. Depending on the application, those values may be sensitive. A controlled internal identifier or appropriately protected audit record can provide correlation without exposing unnecessary financial information in telemetry. There is another useful distinction in this example: the block number is part of the operation's context, not merely a descriptive label. If the agent later creates a transaction based on that observation, the workflow can reference the observation record and evaluate whether the information is still valid for execution. The span tells us which read occurred. The associated decision record tells us why that read mattered.

A trace describes how work moved through the system. A decision record describes the operational basis for a consequential action. I would give every transaction proposal a durable identifier and record the relevant context, policy version, and outcome. The record should contain enough information to reconstruct the decision without depending on the original model conversation remaining available. For example:

The identifiers and block numbers here are fictional. The example illustrates a useful design choice: the agent's decision can be stopped before signing if the application determines that the indexed data does not satisfy the freshness requirement for the intended operation.

The record does not claim that every two-block difference is unsafe. Whether that difference matters depends on the chain, the indexer's behaviour, the transaction, and the application's consistency requirements. A reporting agent might accept the indexed observation. An agent preparing a price-sensitive swap might require a newer observation or an independent validation step. The decision record should make the distinction explicit. It should also be updated as the operation progresses, or linked to append-only lifecycle events, so that the system can distinguish between a proposal, an authorisation, a submission, and a verified outcome.

For high-impact operations, I prefer a design in which the authorisation event is separately recorded and bound to the exact transaction parameters. This reduces the risk that a proposal will be changed after it passes validation. A record should never be treated as proof that an action occurred merely because it says the action was intended. The execution evidence must be independently established.

One of the most common mistakes in monitoring is treating every unsuccessful operation as the same kind of failure. A failed RPC request, an agent decision rejected by policy, a transaction that reverts, and a successful transaction that produces the wrong business outcome are fundamentally different events. They require different responses. I would classify failures by the layer where they occur and the evidence needed to resolve them.

Refresh, reconcile, or reject the decision

The proposal does not satisfy the task constraints

Reject the proposal and investigate the planning failure

Block execution and record the violated rule

Apply bounded retry or use an approved alternative source

The transaction remains pending or is replaced

Reconcile the known transaction state before taking action

Inspect the receipt and relevant execution details

Transaction succeeds, but the intended result is not achieved

Trigger investigation and an application-specific recovery process

Required telemetry or audit evidence is missing

Raise a monitoring-integrity alert and apply the appropriate fail-safe policy

The category alone does not determine the response. A timeout might be transient, while a timeout during transaction submission may leave the outcome uncertain. A policy rejection may be the correct behaviour rather than an incident. The system should preserve the distinction between an expected refusal, a recoverable operational failure, and a security-relevant anomaly. This is particularly important for AI agents. If a system is evaluated only on its task-completion rate, it may appear that policy rejections are failures to be eliminated. In reality, a correctly rejected unsafe transaction can be a sign that the controls are working.

The right metric is not simply how often the agent completes a task. It is whether the system completes legitimate tasks while reliably preventing unauthorised or invalid actions.

An AI-native blockchain dashboard should help an operator answer three questions quickly:

I would organise the dashboard around those questions rather than presenting every available metric on one screen. The first view should show operational health: RPC latency, provider errors, indexer lag, agent task latency, queue depth, and transaction lifecycle distribution. The second should focus on decision integrity: stale-context rejections, inconsistent-observation detections, policy rejection reasons, simulation failures, and the proportion of transaction proposals requiring refresh or human approval. The third should focus on outcomes: pending transactions, confirmed execution results, reverted transactions, unresolved submissions, and mismatches between intended and observed state changes.

The following chart illustrates how a dashboard might compare decision outcomes over a hypothetical monitoring period. These are invented figures for demonstration, not measurements from a deployed system.

The value of this chart is not the particular proportions. Real systems will vary significantly by workload, protocol, and risk policy. The useful idea is that a single task success percentage conceals several different operational states.

For example, an increase in refresh-required proposals may indicate that an indexer is falling behind, that the application's freshness threshold is too strict, or that the workload has become more sensitive to rapidly changing data. A rise in unresolved submissions may indicate RPC instability or a problem with transaction-state reconciliation.

The dashboard should make it possible to move from a metric to the relevant traces and decision records. A number without a path to investigation is often a poor operational tool.

Observability is most useful when it helps teams identify a deteriorating condition before it becomes a serious incident. For blockchain-connected AI agents, I would start with a small set of operational indicators and expand them as the system's risks become better understood.

Context freshness. Measure the age of decision-critical observations at the time a proposal is authorised, not only when the data is retrieved. Where appropriate, measure the difference between the observation's block reference and the relevant indexing checkpoint.

Decision rejection rate. Track proposals rejected because of invalid assumptions, missing information, or policy violations. Break the metric down by reason so that an increase can be investigated rather than treated as a generic failure.

Transaction lifecycle latency. Measure time spent preparing, validating, signing, submitting, waiting for inclusion, and verifying outcomes. This helps distinguish slow agent reasoning from slow blockchain infrastructure.

Unresolved transaction rate. Track operations whose final state cannot yet be established. A pending or uncertain transaction should remain unresolved until the application has sufficient evidence to classify it.

Outcome mismatch rate. Measure how often an operation reaches a technically successful execution state without achieving its defined application-level objective.

Audit completeness. Measure whether consequential actions have the required decision, authorisation, transaction, and outcome records. Missing evidence is itself an operational concern.

These metrics should have explicit definitions. For example, an outcome mismatch rate needs a clear definition of success for each operation type. A token transfer may be verified through the relevant transaction and state changes, while a more complex DeFi operation may require several application-specific checks. Thresholds should also be established from the application's risk model and observed baseline rather than copied from an unrelated system.

I would avoid optimising the entire platform around one composite reliability score. Averages can hide rare but serious failures. A low average latency does not compensate for an unsafe transaction, and a high task-completion rate does not establish that authorisation controls are effective. For critical controls, direct measurements of violations and execution outcomes are more useful than a single headline number.

An observability platform can contain valuable information about how an AI agent operates, which contracts it interacts with, what policies constrain it, and how its execution infrastructure is configured. That information needs protection.

Logging every prompt, tool response, wallet identifier, and transaction parameter without considering their sensitivity can expose financial activity or reveal details that attackers could use to target the system. I would apply data minimisation at the instrumentation layer. Record the information required to understand a decision, but avoid collecting private keys, signing credentials, recovery phrases, or other secrets. Sensitive prompt content and user information should be redacted or access-controlled according to the application's requirements.

High-cardinality fields also deserve attention. Putting arbitrary wallet addresses, transaction hashes, or user identifiers into metric labels can cause monitoring systems to consume excessive memory and storage. These values are generally better suited to trace attributes or structured records than to unrestricted metric dimensions.

Audit integrity is another consideration. A system should make it difficult for an ordinary agent process to alter or delete the records of its own consequential actions. Depending on the threat model, this can involve append-only storage, restricted write permissions, integrity checks, and separation between the execution service and the audit service.

A hash-linked audit log can help detect certain forms of modification, but it does not automatically prove that the recorded events are complete or truthful. If the application fails to record an event in the first place, an integrity mechanism cannot reconstruct it.

Finally, observability must not silently become a dependency that fails open. If the system cannot produce a required authorisation record for a high-impact transaction, it may need to block execution or require a controlled fallback. For a low-risk reporting task, temporary telemetry loss might instead trigger an alert while the task continues. The correct response depends on the risk and on which records are essential to safe operation.

A full observability platform can become complicated quickly. It is tempting to instrument every service, define dozens of metrics, and build a large dashboard before understanding which questions the team actually needs to answer. I would start with one consequential workflow and instrument it end-to-end.

For example, select a transaction-preparation workflow that reads contract state, generates a proposal, applies policy checks, and submits an authorised transaction. Assign a stable workflow identifier, connect the relevant spans, and record the minimum decision and execution evidence.

Next, introduce controlled failure tests. Simulate an unavailable RPC provider, an indexer that falls behind, a policy rejection, a reverted transaction, and a submission timeout. Confirm that each scenario produces a distinct classification and that engineers can reconstruct the workflow without manually searching unrelated logs.

Then introduce the dashboard and define the expected behaviour for unresolved states. Ensure that an uncertain submission cannot trigger a duplicate transaction simply because an agent assumes the previous attempt failed. Only after these basics work would I expand the architecture to additional workflows and services. This approach makes observability an engineering capability that grows with the system rather than a separate reporting project. It also gives the team something measurable to improve: fewer unexplained failures, faster incident investigation, more complete decision records, and stronger evidence that authorisation and execution behave as intended.

As AI agents become more capable of interacting with financial infrastructure, the meaning of a successful operation will need to become more precise. A successful model response does not necessarily mean that a valid transaction was proposed. A successful RPC call does not mean that a transaction was confirmed. A confirmed transaction does not necessarily mean that the user's intended outcome was achieved.

Each stage needs its own evidence, and those stages need to remain connected. This is the architectural shift I find most important: moving from monitoring individual components to observing the complete lifecycle of an autonomous decision.

Blockchain explorers will continue to provide valuable visibility into on-chain activity. Application logs will continue to explain local execution. Distributed traces will continue to connect work across services. But AI-driven applications need an additional layer that connects those sources to the intent, constraints, and outcome of each consequential action.

That layer must also recognise its own limits. Observability can help engineers understand what happened, detect unexpected behaviour, and improve recovery. It cannot guarantee that an agent will never make a bad decision, replace a sound authorisation model, or reverse a transaction that has already been confirmed.

Its purpose is to make the system's behaviour sufficiently visible that problems can be detected, investigated, and addressed before uncertainty becomes an unmanaged operational risk. For me, this is one of the important engineering challenges in moving AI beyond demonstrations and into production. The more autonomy we introduce, the less acceptable it becomes to treat the final output as the only evidence that matters.

We need to observe not just what the agent did, but the path from its intended action to the verified result. In blockchain applications, that path crosses probabilistic reasoning, external data, policy decisions, distributed services, and deterministic execution. Making those boundaries visible is what turns observability from a collection of dashboards into a foundation for operating autonomous systems responsibly.

The next generation of AI infrastructure will need to make these systems not only capable of acting, but also understandable when their actions do not go as planned.

#9772. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

I wonder how many other agencies have the same exposure and just have not been named yet. Proxy SDKs bundled into free apps are hard to spot, so an inventory of apps on managed devices would be a sensible first step.

If the software allows 3rd parties to exit the device then the 3rd parties (or at a minimum those who control the software itself) have internal access too.

#9770. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

#9768. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9767. DeepSeek's Super-Agent Moves the Attention Bottleneck From Your Feed to Your Agents

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

On November 1, 2026, the DeepSeek Harness team posted a technical essay, "Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System." A day later, Jen Zhu Scott quote-posted it with one line: "This is an obituary for Attention Economy."

That is a big claim for an engineering document. The essay never mentions ad markets, feeds or scrolling. It argues about agent architecture. But its core diagnosis, that human attention, not model capability, now caps how much work agents can do in parallel, pokes at the same scarce resource the ad-funded internet has monetized for two decades. To see why the line lands, and where it overreaches, start with the layer DeepSeek is redesigning: the harness.

An agent is not a model. The shorthand that spread in early 2026 is agent = model + harness, a formula the academic literature credits to LangChain's engineering writing. The model predicts tokens. The harness turns those predictions into multi-step action: the loop that keeps calling the model, the tools it may invoke, the context and memory it sees, the permission system that decides what runs freely and what waits for approval, the orchestration of sub-agents, and the extension points (skills, plugins, MCP servers, hooks) that let the system grow without a rewrite.

A July 2026 source-code study of eleven production coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Aider and Hermes, read roughly four million lines of code and found the same seven subsystems in every one: agent loop, LLM integration, tools, memory and context, safety, orchestration and extensibility. None of them import a general-purpose agent framework, and the SKILL.md format now shows up in more of them (9 of 11) than MCP (8 of 11). The paper, Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents, closes with 18 design recommendations and a 90-line starter harness that implements ten of them. HackerNoon writers have been circling the same conclusion: agent reliability depends more on the harness than the model.

Developer NO1ennn read that paper and called harness engineering "the most f*cking DANGEROUS and accessible thing" he had ever seen. Both adjectives describe the same fact. Ninety lines buy a loop that can touch the filesystem, the terminal and the network. The model is rented or open-weight. The harness is the part you own, and the part that decides what the model may do when nobody is watching.

The scaffolding mattered before it had a name. ReAct-style reasoning loops and the 2024 SWE-agent paper showed that redesigning the agent-computer interface could move benchmark scores as much as swapping the model. Practitioners spent years building system prompts, tool schemas, permission policies and sandboxes without a shared term for the work.

The term arrived in early 2026. The Wavestone researchers behind the source-code study credit Mitchell Hashimoto with first using "harness engineering" in passing and LangChain's Vivek Trivedy with defining it. Hashimoto's version is practical: every time an agent makes a mistake, engineer a permanent fix into its environment so the mistake cannot recur. By mid-2026 the harness was an object of academic study, and DeepSeek pushed the idea to its limit with DeepSeek Harness, where even the agent loop is a plugin. There is no privileged core to patch.

NO1ennn's own long-form post shows what this looks like at night. He built the harness around his agent (context, tools, loop, evals, rules) but hated running his 412-eval suite every evening and triaging the failures. So he gave the night shift to an agent named Viktor: run the suite at 2 AM, compare failures with the night before, propose fixes as pull requests, and "do not merge or change anything on your own." Viktor prepares. A human signs. That one constraint separates a tool that runs when you run it from a system that owns a job while a person keeps signature authority.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is an MIT-licensed, model-agnostic agent runtime whose README sums up its design as "Everything is a Plugin": the model adapter, tool registry, session log, sandbox, scheduler, UI and the agent loop itself. It runs on the Cordis plugin framework and launches as a local web UI with a single npx command. The repo now shows more than 270,000 GitHub stars.

The November essay, written by Yujia Qiao of the Harness team, names the single session as the next bottleneck. Models now finish complex tasks with less steering, so the constraint has moved. "A single task is limited by model capability, but multi-tasking is limited by human attention," the team wrote, adding that a person can actively track only three to five concurrent sessions. Past that point, more capable agents add context-switching costs instead of output.

The proposed Super-agent has four properties: continuous, productive, proactive and persistent. It is reachable across chat apps and GitHub comments without the user tracking sessions, it runs parallel tasks, it reacts to events without being prompted, and it recovers from failures. Architecturally, a long-lived Router session handles the human conversation and dispatches isolated Worker sessions for individual tasks. DeepSeek also contrasts its approach with Anthropic's "Decoupling the brain from the hands," noting that its design must first connect personal computers that are often only intermittently online.

The team released an MIT-licensed research prototype alongside the essay. In simulated workloads, the Super-agent finished tasks at a median of 12.4 minutes versus 20.4 minutes for a single-session agent. DeepSeek calls it "only a prototype for validating the technical approach, not an official DeepSeek product."

The idea traces to Herbert Simon's 1971 observation that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. For most of history, information was scarce. Once computers, networks and mass media reversed that, attention became the binding constraint.

In the 1990s, Michael Goldhaber's Wired essay "Attention Shoppers!" turned the observation into an economic claim: attention, more than information or even money, would become the real currency of cyberspace. Goldhaber described a pure attention economy of stars and fans. The commercial internet built something narrower: ad-funded platforms engineering notifications, recommendation feeds and infinite scroll to maximize time-on-site, then selling access to that time. HackerNoon contributors have argued that focus is becoming the class divide of this century for exactly that reason.

Almost not at all. The Super-agent is a prototype released days ago. Its benchmarks use simulated workloads, not real multi-user environments. DeepSeek Harness has serious developer traction as infrastructure, but it does not compete with consumer platforms or ad markets.

The idea is landing, though, while other arguments converge on the same weak point. IEEE Spectrum reports that digital advertisers may soon compete for AI agents' attention rather than humans'. Economists have modeled an "attention lemons" problem in two-sided ad markets once agents do the browsing. California Management Review describes a "trust economy" in which agents rewrite the rules of digital strategy. And on HackerNoon, one writer argues that AI coding already created a new attention market, while another warns that multitasking across coding agents drains the attention it was meant to save.

None of this dents Meta, Google, TikTok or the open-web ad stack this week. What changed is the recognition, visible in both DeepSeek's essay and NO1ennn's night shift, that the scarce resource is no longer only the hours a person spends scrolling. It is also the hours a person spends supervising the agents that were supposed to free those hours.

The same 90-line starter that makes harness engineering accessible makes it dangerous. A model without a harness is a chat window. A model with a good harness can read private files, run shell commands, open pull requests, send messages, schedule recurring work and recover from its own failures. The Super-agent hides the session-management tax so one person can keep more of that work in flight. Open, trivial-to-start harnesses plus architectures that demand less supervision lower the barrier to deploying systems with persistence and reach.

Viktor's "do not merge or change anything on your own" is one careful answer. It is not a prompt trick but a hard boundary in the harness: every action that matters waits for a human yes. Today the person who built the harness enforces that boundary. As Super-agent-style systems grow more continuous and proactive, the open question is whether the boundary stays a deliberate engineering choice or erodes under the pressure of "just let it finish."

Accessibility also means failure modes are no longer confined to well-funded labs. Anyone who can write a SKILL.md, configure a plugin or fork a 90-line loop can hand a model real-world effectors. Safety is one of the seven canonical subsystems precisely because the other six can do damage. When the harness is the product, its bugs are capability bugs: a context window that silently drops a constraint, a tool description that is slightly too broad, a permission policy that fails open. HackerNoon's own chronicle of the period, The Age of the Lobster, catalogs how quickly those effectors spread.

The structural question is more interesting. Today's agent interfaces keep the session as the unit of work: open a chat, assign a task, watch it, switch contexts, restate goals. The human is the router. The Super-agent moves routing into the system so the person works at the level of decisions and approvals. If that pattern spreads, three things follow.

First, attention per unit of work falls. DeepSeek's team says plainly that the bottleneck to further productivity is shifting toward human attention. A continuous agent that dispatches parallel work and surfaces results only when judgment is needed attacks the assumption that more capable agents must consume proportionally more human attention.

Second, the main consumer of interfaces may change. When agents browse, compare, buy and coordinate for us, value flows to interfaces that are machine-readable and criteria-satisfying rather than sticky. Content built for emotional engagement or variable-reward notifications matters less if the agent never scrolls. Media companies will face pressure to publish material that agents can parse, trust and act on.

Third, attention gets reallocated, not abolished. Goldhaber's point was that people's appetite for attention has no upper bound. Freeing attention from low-level monitoring raises the value of what remains for high-stakes judgment, relationships and creative work. Others warn of an "intention economy", in which platforms move upstream from capturing attention to forecasting and selling intentions before users fully form them.

The counter-forces are real. Ad and recommendation systems will adapt. Platforms can still monetize the moments when humans review agent output, set goals or resolve ambiguity. Synthetic agents that mimic human engagement can pollute metrics. Coordination between agents remains harder than individual competence. The harness layer simply moves the scarce resource one level up: from the content that captures attention to the systems that decide what agents attend to on our behalf.

Platforms engineering for maximum human engagement still dominate. The prototype has not proven it scales, its tests are synthetic, and the ad infrastructure is vast. Obituaries get written after the fact. This is a design document.

It is, however, a precise diagnosis of a moving bottleneck and a concrete architectural response. "Multi-tasking is limited by human attention" names the same scarcity Simon described in 1971, now appearing inside the agent stack. If systems that route work, act proactively and need less supervision become the default interface to the digital world, the logic that rewards capturing human attention for its own sake loses force. Value moves toward systems that satisfy agent criteria, earn trust for delegated action and give attention back.

Harness engineering makes that shift more accessible and more dangerous at once. Open-source runtimes lower the cost of giving a model real effectors. The Super-agent lowers the ongoing attention cost of keeping them running. Together they move the scarce resource from "who can capture human eyes" to "who designs the boundaries that still require a human yes." NO1ennn kept the signature. Whether that stays the default or becomes a setting most people switch off is the question the next few years of harness design will answer.

#9766. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9765. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

Get more tips for holiday success in our Thanksgiving Baking Guide.

#9763. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:
